newsitem.title: HONG KONG: A Hong Kong street of life-events ignores history.
newsitem.headline: A Hong Kong street of life-events ignores history.

text.p: A 30-minute walk separates the beginning and end of British rule in Hong Kong.
At the start, life's milestones like funerals and weddings preoccupy Chinese traders around Possession Street, where imperial conquest is ignored or forgotten.
The little sloping street was a coastal promontory when a British naval party landed and claimed Hong Kong in the name of Queen Victoria in 1841.
Now, the beginning and end of colonial Hong Kong are easily connected.
A 30-minute stroll from Possession Street, through skyscraper canyons, Queen Elizabeth's heir, Prince Charles, hands Hong Kong back to China at midnight.

The sovereignty transfer takes place in a gleaming new Convention Centre at the harbourside on reclaimed land, a symbol of how this rocky, treeless place, lacking resources, has become a world financial centre through skill and hard work.
To local and visiting Chinese, Possession Street, reached by way of Hollywood Road, is an obscure place in the western part of Hong Kong.
It has an entirely different name in Chinese characters -- Water Channel Street, giving no hint of its significance.

Apart from the two English words on the bilingual street signs, the twilight of British rule sees no monuments in an area where craftsmen make coffins and decorations for funeral and wedding ceremonies. They include banknotes for the dead in the next world and scarlet good luck finery for newlyweds.
Here, where it all started, the imperial legacy has long faded. An astonished television crew from Beijing eagerly seeks out bystanders for comment about the street's background.

The replies come in a steady flow...Don't know...don't recall...not sure. Of half a dozen people questioned at random, only one, an elderly man, comes close: "The British came here, long ago, before my time. Not sure when."

Can Ch Him manages a lucrative shop selling swallow nests from Indonesia, for use in the Chinese delicacy, bird's nest soup. He recalls his father talking of a time when the British conquest was still a memory to some.
Now 51, he says Possession Street has declined from a bustling area of restaurants, flower stalls, and antique shops.

Of its Chinese name, he says: "My father's generation told me there was a water channel running through the street which was on the waterfront and here was where the British first landed. Our shop was originally by the seaside.
"There is a decrease in the number of people living here. A lot of people have gone. The night market was prosperous, now there is none. It was once the most prosperous area in western region."

Walk northeast through a maze of streets, hectic with Chinese signs and banners, and you reach the gleaming steel-and-glass Convention Centre, its giant, curved roof intended to suggest the flight of a bird and the ascendancy of Hong Kong as a vibrant hub of East Asia.
The HK$4.8 billion (US$620 million) convention centre is built on a 6.5 hectare (16 acre) man-made island in Victoria Harbour, just off the Central District waterfront.

Here at midnight (1600 GMT), watched by the world, the great-great-grandson of Queen Victoria was to hand back Hong Kong to President Jiang Zemin of China, ending an imperial adventure and one and a half centuries of Chinese shame.
